To ensnare someone or something means to trap them — usually through clever, cunning, or deceptive means — in a way that makes it very difficult to escape.

The word carries two layers that always work together: capture + deception. It's not just about trapping something. It's about trapping something sneakily, often without the victim realizing what is happening until it's too late.

To truly understand this word, picture an animal trap set in a forest. A hunter quietly lays a snare — a hidden wire loop on the ground — and waits. A rabbit comes along, completely unaware, steps into the loop, and suddenly finds itself caught. It didn't walk into an obvious cage. It was lured in without knowing, and now it cannot get free.

That image is the heartbeat of "ensnare."

Now, "ensnare" is simply the verb built from that same idea: to do the act of catching something in a snare. In its most literal sense, it means to catch an animal using a trap. But in everyday modern use, this literal meaning is rare. What you'll almost always see is the figurative use — applied to people, situations, and abstract ideas.
The Figurative (and Far More Common) Meaning

When used figuratively — which is how this word is used most of the time — to ensnare someone means to trap a person in a situation, relationship, scheme, feeling, or problem from which they struggle to break free. Crucially, the trapping usually happens through trickery, manipulation, gradual involvement, or some kind of bait, just like a physical snare uses bait to lure an animal.

The person being ensnared often:

  • doesn't see it coming
  • doesn't fully realize they are trapped until they're already deep in
  • finds it very hard to get out once caught
The Tone and Feel of the Word

Ensnare is almost always negative. It implies that something bad — or at least unwanted — is happening to the person being trapped. There is a strong sense of loss of freedom, loss of control, and helplessness.

The one doing the ensnaring is usually portrayed as scheming, manipulative, or at least calculating. Even when no human is doing the trapping (for example, when someone is ensnared by debt or by addiction), the word still suggests that the trap was subtle and hard to see coming.
Examples That Show the Full Range

Here are examples showing how "ensnare" works across different situations. Read each one carefully — notice how the idea of "hidden trap + loss of freedom" is present every time.

1. A criminal scheme:

"The con artist ensnared dozens of elderly victims with promises of easy money."

The victims were deceived. They didn't know they were walking into a trap. Now they've lost their savings and can't easily undo the damage.

2. A toxic relationship:

"She felt ensnared in a relationship she no longer wanted but couldn't seem to leave."

She didn't enter the relationship expecting to feel trapped. Over time, she found herself unable to get out — emotionally, financially, or socially. She is caught.

3. A legal or political trap:

"The politician was ensnared by his own lies when journalists uncovered the truth."

His own deception became the trap. The lies he told to protect himself ended up catching him.

4. Debt or addiction:

"Millions of people are ensnared by debt before they even realize how serious the situation has become."

No single person tricked them, but the situation itself acted like a hidden snare — subtle at first, then impossible to ignore.

5. A seductive idea or feeling:

"He was completely ensnared by greed, and it led to his downfall."

Greed crept in slowly, wrapped around him, and wouldn't let go. He was a prisoner of his own desire.
What Makes "Ensnare" Different from Similar Words

Many words are related to trapping, but "ensnare" has a very specific personality.

  • Trap is more general and neutral. A trap can be obvious. Ensnaring always implies something hidden and deceptive.
  • Catch is completely neutral — you can catch a ball, catch a criminal, catch a bus. No deception is implied.
  • Lure focuses on the bait used to attract someone. Ensnare focuses on the capture itself — the moment of being caught and held.
  • Entangle suggests getting caught up in something messy and complicated (like being entangled in legal problems), but doesn't strongly imply that someone deliberately set a trap for you. Ensnare almost always implies deliberateness or at least a hidden danger.
  • Ensnare sits at the intersection of all of these: deliberate + deceptive + capturing + hard to escape. That precise combination is what makes it unique.
The Grammar: How to Use It

"Ensnare" is a transitive verb, which means it always acts on an object — something or someone is always being ensnared.

Common patterns:

  • Ensnare + someone: "The scam ensnared thousands of people."
  • Be ensnared by + something: "She was ensnared by false promises."
  • Be ensnared in + something: "He was ensnared in a web of lies."
  • Ensnare + someone + in + something: "They ensnared him in a scheme he didn't understand."

Notice the two prepositions: "by" is used when pointing to the cause or the thing trapping you; "in" is used when pointing to the situation or web you are caught inside. Both are correct and common.

If you need to remember just one thing: to ensnare is to trap something or someone cleverly and deceptively, in a way that makes escape very difficult — whether that's an animal in a wire loop, a person in a scam, or a soul caught in its own unchecked desires.
